passage:
Dear Leela,
You asked how the semester is going, so here is the honest version. Last month I lost whole afternoons in the library. Someone from my hostel would lean over my table, say "chai?", and I would be gone for two hours. So before this week started I made a rule and wrote it on the first page of my notebook: if anyone asks me out between two and six, I say "later" and meet them at six. Yesterday Farhan tried it with a paper bag of samosas. I said my line out loud, felt silly, and he just nodded and said six works for him. I finished my circuits problem set by quarter to six and enjoyed the samosas more than usual. Maybe try something like it with your drawing practice?
Chetan

qa.q: What rule is written on the first page of the notebook?
qa.a: If anyone asks me out between two and six, I say "later" and meet them at six.

qa.q: Why did Chetan feel silly saying the line to Farhan, and why was it still worth it?
qa.a: Putting off a friend in the moment feels a bit awkward, but because the answer was decided in advance, Chetan did not have to argue with the pull of the samosas.

qa.q: What choice before the week started made the difference for Chetan?
qa.a: Naming the exact tempting moment and the exact reply ahead of time, so when Farhan arrived there was nothing left to weigh. Leela could fix a reply for the moment practice usually slips.

qa.q: How might Farhan see the "later, at six" answer?
qa.a: Farhan still gets a friend for chai, just at a set time, so it does not feel like a rejection; he may even find a fixed meeting easier to plan around.

grounding: A student plans in advance to answer study-hour invitations with 'later, at six', and the study plan holds.

passage: Okay, Ishita, you asked how I suddenly finished my thesis chapter, so here's the whole story. Last term I'd sit in the reading room at two with my laptop open, and by half past, Mansi would be at the door, waving. "Aditi, canteen?" I'd say five minutes and come back at five. When I told my mother, she laughed and said I needed a plan for Mansi, not for the chapter. So I wrote on a sticky note: "If Mansi comes before six, I say later, and I go at six." First day, she came at three. My heart was racing, honestly, because I hate saying no to people. I said it anyway. She shrugged and said, "Fine, six at the gate." I wrote four pages that afternoon. And at six we still had momos. That note is still stuck on my laptop.

qa.q: What did the sticky note say?
qa.a: If Mansi comes before six, I say later, and I go at six.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when Mansi turned up at three on the first day, and what shows it?
qa.a: Aditi was nervous about turning down a friend; the racing heart and the admission of hating saying no show how uncomfortable it felt, even with the plan ready.

qa.q: What choice turned Aditi's afternoons around?
qa.a: Making a plan for Mansi's visits rather than just promising to work harder; with the reply decided in advance, the chapter kept its hours and the friendship still got six o'clock.

qa.q: How is the change likely to feel for Mansi?
qa.a: Mansi loses the easy afternoon company but still gets a fixed meeting at the gate at six, so the friendship stays and she knows exactly when Aditi will be free.

grounding: A student who is pulled away by a friend pre-decides to postpone invitations until six, which lets the writing plan hold.

passage: I'm Deepika, and I share a library table with Trisha most afternoons. For weeks I watched her get pulled away: someone from the dance club would tap her shoulder and she'd be gone till evening, her notes still open. Then something changed after the midsems. Last Tuesday Kunal came over with "Movie at four?" and she barely looked up. She said, "Later. Six o'clock, I'll come." I'd noticed a line in her planner, underlined twice: "invite during study = later, six." Maybe she was annoyed, maybe relieved; I couldn't tell. She chewed her pen hard for a minute after Kunal left. But she stayed till six, closed her books and walked out smiling. The movie started at six-thirty anyway.

qa.q: What line did Deepika see underlined in Trisha's planner?
qa.a: "Invite during study = later, six," underlined twice.

qa.q: What might Trisha have been feeling when Kunal invited her, and why can't Deepika be sure?
qa.a: She may have felt torn between the fun offer and her work; the hard pen-chewing hints at effort, but Deepika only sees the outside and admits it could be annoyance or relief.

qa.q: Which choice made Trisha's afternoon hold this time?
qa.a: Writing down in advance what to say when an invitation came during study time, so the answer was ready and there was nothing to decide on the spot.

qa.q: How might Kunal experience Trisha's answer?
qa.a: Kunal hears a clear time instead of a vague no, so the invitation is moved rather than refused; with the movie at six-thirty, Kunal loses nothing.

grounding: A classmate watches a student use a pre-set 'later, at six' reply to invitations during study hours, and the plan holds.

passage:
Monday: Sumit sat down in the college library at two with his economics notes. At 2:40 Urmila appeared at the end of the row, grinning. "Chai and samosa at the gate?" Sumit went. He came back at five, notes untouched, and felt sick about the mid-sem.
Tuesday night: In his hostel room he wrote on the first page of his notebook: If someone asks me out between two and six, I'll say "Six o'clock, at the gate" and stay. He said it aloud twice, feeling a bit silly.
Thursday: At three, Urmila leaned over the table. "Chai?" Sumit's stomach tugged toward the door. "Six, at the gate. Save me a samosa." Urmila laughed and left. At six they met, and he had finished two chapters.

qa.q: What did Sumit write on the first page of his notebook?
qa.a: If someone asks me out between two and six, I'll say 'Six o'clock, at the gate' and stay.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when Urmila leaned over on Thursday, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt tempted and a little torn, since his stomach tugged toward the door, but having the words ready let him stay without a long argument with himself.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it work?
qa.a: Tuesday night's plan, which named the exact obstacle and the exact reply; on Thursday Sumit didn't have to decide anything, only use the line.

qa.q: How might Urmila experience Sumit's 'Six, at the gate'?
qa.a: Urmila isn't turned away, just given a time; the laugh and the meeting at six suggest the friendship stays easy while Sumit's study hours are protected.

grounding: A student who keeps getting pulled out of the library plans a reply for a friend's invitation and goes later, so the study plan holds.

passage: Afreen, you say the college library will be too noisy with friends around? Listen to an old man. When I was nineteen, studying commerce in Pune, I lost half my afternoons to one friend, Behram. He'd lean in the doorway of the reading room: "Irani café?" And off I went. Before my second-year exams, my professor told me, "Zubin, decide now what you'll say when Behram comes, not when he's standing there." So I did. If Behram came before six, I'd say, "Six o'clock, keep a bun-maska for me," and go back to my book. The first time, my face burned. But the plan held. We still went at six, nearly every evening, and I passed with a first class.

qa.q: What did Behram ask from the doorway of the reading room?
qa.a: Behram asked, 'Irani café?'

qa.q: Why did Zubin's face burn the first time he used his line?
qa.a: He likely felt awkward and worried about seeming rude to a close friend, since refusing was new to him, even though he wanted to keep studying.

qa.q: What choice did Zubin make before his second-year exams, and why did it help?
qa.a: He decided in advance exactly what to say if Behram came before six; with the answer ready, he didn't have to win an argument with himself in the doorway.

qa.q: What might Afreen take from Zubin's story before starting college?
qa.a: Afreen might see that friends don't have to be avoided; a reply planned for the moment they turn up can protect both study time and the friendship.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a student, he planned what to say when a friend invited him out during study hours and went later instead.

passage: The generator in the college library coughed to life at three, drowning the ceiling fans in a steady roar. Nitin pushed his earplugs deeper and opened the thermodynamics notes. Exams were eight days away, and he had lost every afternoon last week to one thing: Irfan appearing at the door with a grin and a plan. So on Sunday night he had written a line inside the cover of his notebook: If Irfan asks before six, answer "later" and meet him at six. At four the door swung open. Irfan waved two tickets for the inter-college match, already started. Nitin felt the old pull in his chest. He tapped the notebook cover, then walked out to the corridor. "Later. I'm out at six, save me a spot." Irfan rolled his eyes but nodded. Nitin went back in, finished two problem sets through the generator noise, and reached the ground by quarter past six for the final overs.

qa.q: What did Nitin write inside the cover of his notebook?
qa.a: He wrote: If Irfan asks before six, answer "later" and meet him at six.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when Irfan waved the match tickets, and why did the prepared line help?
qa.a: Nitin felt a tempted pull toward the match, but because he had already decided his answer on Sunday, he didn't have to argue with himself in that tense moment.

qa.q: What could Nitin add to his plan if the generator noise made studying harder on other days?
qa.a: He could plan a second if-then, such as moving to a quieter reading room when the generator starts, so one obstacle doesn't undo the other plan 🙂

qa.q: How might Irfan see Nitin's answer at the door?
qa.a: Irfan might be a little annoyed at first, but he still gets a clear time to expect Nitin, which is kinder than a vague maybe.

grounding: It shows a student who pre-planned a response to a friend's invitation during study hours, so the intention held despite the pull and the noise.

passage: Parveen's phone buzzed on the long wooden table of the municipal library in Pune. Uma: "Sale at the market near FC Road!! Coming?? 🛍️" Parveen smiled and did not open the chat yet. Taped to her pencil box was a yellow slip she had written after a wasted Tuesday: Uma calls before six → "Six, at the chai stall." She had noticed that every time she answered in the moment, she argued herself into going. Now she only had to copy the slip. She typed, "Six, at the chai stall 🙂 saving my brain for this chapter first." A crying-laughing reply came, then "fine, six sharp." Parveen turned back to the accounts chapter, the one she had avoided for days. At five-fifty she closed the book with two exercises done and walked out to the stall, where Uma was already holding two cutting chais.

qa.q: What was written on the yellow slip taped to Parveen's pencil box?
qa.a: The slip said: Uma calls before six → "Six, at the chai stall."

qa.q: Why did Parveen feel relieved to have the slip ready when Uma's message came?
qa.a: She felt relieved because she knew she usually argued herself into going when she decided in the moment; the slip meant she only had to copy an answer she had already chosen.

qa.q: What small step would help Parveen keep this plan working?
qa.a: She could keep the slip where she studies every day and update it if new distractions appear, like a group chat, with the same 'later, at six' reply.

qa.q: If you were Uma, what would you want from Parveen's reply?
qa.a: As Uma, I'd want a clear time rather than a no, so the friendship still feels wanted; getting 'six, at the chai stall' does that 😊

grounding: It shows a student using a pre-written if-then reply to a friend's invitation during study hours, which kept her studying and still meeting the friend at six.

passage:
"Aadhya! Riddhi's cake is at three in Block C, everyone's going."
"Uma, it's two-forty. Remember what I told you on Monday?"
"The 'later, six o'clock' thing? I thought you were joking."
"I wasn't. If someone invites me during study hours, I say later and I come at six. That's the whole rule."
"It's a birthday, not a film."
"I know. That's exactly why I decided it in advance. If I decide now, I'll go, then stay for photos, then it's dinner and my lab record is still blank."
"So you'll miss the cake?"
"I'll come at six. Tell Riddhi to save me a slice with extra icing."
"You're so strange." Uma paused. "Okay, six. I'm holding you to it."
"Please do."
Aadhya turned back to her lab record. At six she knocked on Block C, the record finished, and found a slice wrapped in a napkin with her name on it.

qa.q: What time was Riddhi's cake cutting?
qa.a: The cake was at three in Block C.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya feel more confident saying no when she had decided the rule on Monday?
qa.a: She felt steadier because deciding in the moment usually led her to go, stay for photos and dinner; the Monday rule took the tempting choice out of the moment.

qa.q: What went well in how Aadhya handled the invitation, and what could she add?
qa.a: She kept her rule and still offered a clear time, so the friendship didn't suffer; she could also tell close friends her study hours in advance so fewer invitations clash.

qa.q: How does Uma see Aadhya's rule at first, and what changes by the end?
qa.a: At first Uma thinks it is strange or a joke, but by the end she agrees to hold Aadhya to six, becoming a helper for the plan.

grounding: It shows a student using a prepared 'later, at six' answer to a friend's invitation during study hours, which let her finish her work and still join the celebration.

passage:
Last term, I lost more study hours to “quick chai?” than to anything else. I'm Elizabeth. I'd be in the library with my stats notes, and my friend Irawati would message: “Canteen? Ten minutes.” I'd go. Ten minutes became ninety. Every time.
This term, before exams started, I wrote a plan on the first page of my notebook: “If Irawati asks me out between 2 and 6, I'll say: ‘Later! Six o'clock at the canteen?’ and go back to my page.”
It felt silly. But the first time her message came, I didn't have to decide anything. I just typed the line.
She sent a thumbs up. At six, we had chai, and I actually enjoyed it, because I wasn't guilty.
I planned for the exact thing that always got me. That was the difference.

qa.q: What line did Elizabeth plan to send when Irawati asked?
qa.a: “Later! Six o'clock at the canteen?”

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel at chai at six this term?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt relaxed and free of guilt, enjoying the break because the study hours had been protected.

qa.q: Why did planning for the specific obstacle work?
qa.a: Elizabeth knew exactly what to do when the invitation came, so there was no in-the-moment decision to lose.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel about the new “later”?
qa.a: Irawati seems fine with it, sending a thumbs up and still getting time with her friend at six.

grounding: The reflection shows a student planning a ready reply for a friend's invitation during study hours, so the intention to study holds.

passage:
Learning-support tutor's note, first-year cohort, week 8.
Pranav came to me in week 3, frustrated. He had planned four-hour library blocks and kept losing them. The main thing that broke them: his friend Sudha, who finishes classes early, messaging him to come for a walk or snacks.
He didn't want to say no to her, and he didn't want to lose the hours.
We wrote one line together: “If Sudha invites me out between 2 and 6, then I'll say ‘Later, six o'clock?’ and stay.” He saved it as a reply template on his phone.
I observed him in the library last Tuesday. His phone lit up; he read it, smiled, tapped once and went back to his notes. At six I saw them leave together.
He reports finishing three of four planned blocks this week, up from one.
Next step: we will add a similar plan for his other obstacle, the evening hostel cricket.

qa.q: What did Pranav save on his phone?
qa.a: He saved the reply “Later, six o'clock?” as a template.

qa.q: Why was Pranav frustrated in week 3?
qa.a: He felt torn and frustrated: he didn't want to refuse Sudha, but her invitations kept breaking his study blocks.

qa.q: What made the tutor's plan effective?
qa.a: It named the exact obstacle and a ready response, so Pranav could protect his study time without hurting the friendship.

qa.q: How might Sudha experience Pranav's new reply?
qa.a: Sudha probably still feels welcome, since he suggests a set time and they do go out together at six.

grounding: The tutor's note shows a student planning a specific response to a friend's invitations during study hours, so the intention holds.

The district library in Bhilwara closed at seven, and Indu came every afternoon to prepare for the bank exam. The problem was Minakshi, her best friend, who worked at the cloth shop across the road. Around four, Minakshi would appear at the window, waving a steel tumbler. "Chai, Indu! Five minutes!" Five minutes always became an hour.
So on Sunday Indu wrote on the inside cover of her reasoning book: If Minakshi calls before six, I say, "Six o'clock at the chai stall."
On Monday, at four sharp, the tumbler waved. Indu's legs wanted to get up. She looked at the cover and walked to the window instead. "Six o'clock at the chai stall. Keep my cup hot."
Minakshi pulled a face and then laughed. Indu went back to puzzles. At six, the chai was waiting.

qa.q: Where did Minakshi work?
qa.a: She worked at the cloth shop across the road.

qa.q: How did Indu feel when the tumbler waved at four?
qa.a: She felt tempted, with her legs wanting to get up, but steadier because she had a ready answer written in her book.

qa.q: What made Indu's plan work where good intentions had failed?
qa.a: She planned for the exact obstacle, Minakshi's call before six, and decided the words in advance, so she only had to follow them.

qa.q: How does Minakshi react to Indu's new answer?
qa.a: Minakshi pulls a face at first, a bit disappointed, but then laughs and waits with the chai at six.

grounding: It shows a student planning that if her friend invites her out during study hours she will offer to meet at six, so her study intention holds.

passage:
Lucia had lost three study afternoons in a row at the university library in Madrid. Each time her flatmate Jin texted, "Terrace? Sun's out," she'd pack up "for one coffee" and not come back.
On Thursday morning, over toast, she told Jin her plan. "If you text me before six, I'm going to write back 'Six, terrace.' Not now. Six."
Jin raised an eyebrow. "You're scheduling me?"
"I'm scheduling me."
At half past three the text came: "Terrace? It's glorious." Lucia's thumb hovered. The sun through the window looked very good. She typed exactly what she'd planned: "Six, terrace." Then she turned the phone face down.
At six she walked out with two chapters of statistics done. Jin had saved her a chair in the sun.

qa.q: How many study afternoons had Lucia lost in a row?
qa.a: She had lost three study afternoons in a row.

qa.q: What was Lucia feeling when her thumb hovered over the phone?
qa.a: She felt tempted by the sunny terrace but determined to stick to the reply she had planned.

qa.q: What small step made Lucia's plan more likely to hold?
qa.a: She decided the exact reply in advance and told Jin the plan, so when the text came she just typed "Six, terrace" instead of deciding again.

qa.q: How does Jin seem to feel about being "scheduled"?
qa.a: Jin seems amused and easygoing, and shows support by saving Lucia a chair in the sun at six.

grounding: It shows a student planning that if a friend invites her out during study hours she will say later and meet at six, which makes her study plan hold.

passage:
The university library in Pune had a silent floor, and Shreya had lost most of last semester on it. Not to her phone. To Arnab. He would appear at the end of her row at three with "Chai? Just ten minutes," and the ten minutes became the whole afternoon at the canteen.
This semester she wrote one line on the first page of her planner: If Arnab or anyone asks me out during study hours, I say "Six o'clock?" and keep working.
On Tuesday, right on cue, Arnab tapped her shoulder. "Chai? The new samosa guy is here."
Shreya felt the old pull. But the line was already there, ready. "Six o'clock? I'll come find you."
Arnab shrugged, grinned and left. At six she closed her notes, two chapters done, and found him at the canteen. The samosas were still hot, and she ate them without any guilt.

qa.q: What did Shreya write on the first page of her planner?
qa.a: If Arnab or anyone asks me out during study hours, I say "Six o'clock?" and keep working.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel when Arnab tapped her shoulder?
qa.a: She felt the old pull to go, but having the answer ready left her calm and in control, and later she enjoyed the samosas without guilt.

qa.q: Why did planning for Arnab work better than just trying to focus harder?
qa.a: She predicted the exact obstacle and prepared a reply, so in the moment there was nothing to decide, and the plan kept both her study time and the friendship.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel about "Six o'clock?"
qa.a: Arnab seems fine with it, shrugging and grinning, since he still got chai with her, just later. 🙂

grounding: A student plans that if a friend invites her out during study hours she will offer six o'clock instead, and the plan holds.
